plan.analysis: Only evidence is that a constant f gives R=2/3; any improvement must come from a nonuniform shape that makes f*f flatter near its maximum. The best bets are (i) edge-heavy/bathtub profiles that flatten the triangular convolution peak, (ii) direct stochastic shape optimization, and (iii) a smooth low-dimensional search to avoid pixel-level noise. All start from the trivial constant and should spend nearly the full 20 s improving their best construction.

experiments.hypothesis: A symmetric edge-heavy bathtub profile raises convolution mass away from the center just enough to flatten the top of f*f, beating the constant's triangular convolution.
experiments.change: Build h on N=2000 steps using h[i] = 1 + a * |2*(i+0.5)/N - 1|^p, for a grid a in {0,0.1,...,5} and p in {0.5,1,1.5,2,3,5}; also test the center-heavy sign 1 - a*... . Compute exact R from L=[0,*np.convolve(h,h),0] for each, then locally refine the best (a,p) by a short golden-section/bisection scan on a and p. Return the best h.
experiments.prediction: At least one edge-heavy profile with p around 1-3 will score above 0.6667, likely 0.68-0.70; center-heavy profiles will be no better than constant.

experiments.hypothesis: Direct stochastic local search on the step heights can discover non-parametric shapes better than any simple formula.
experiments.change: Use N=512. Initialize by linearly interpolating start onto N=512 if start is given, otherwise ones. Define exact R. Loop until 85% of budget: propose h' = h * exp(sigma*z), where z is a Gaussian-smoothed random vector of length N (smooth with a width-3 kernel), sigma annealed from 0.25 down to 0.003, and occasionally propose a localized block perturbation. Accept if R(h')>R(h); keep the best-ever h. Return the best-ever array scaled to mean 1.
experiments.prediction: This will improve substantially over 2/3, reaching at least 0.70 and probably higher, establishing a non-parametric local-search baseline.

experiments.hypothesis: The optimum profile is smooth, so optimizing a low-dimensional cosine/Chebyshev expansion of log h will find it more reliably than noisy pixel search.
experiments.change: Set x_i=(i+0.5)/N with N=512 and u_i=2*x_i-1. Parameterize log h_i = c0 + sum_{k=1}^{12} c_k T_k(u_i), where T_k are Chebyshev polynomials. Use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead') on objective -R(h), with random initial c vectors in [-1,1], restarting until 85% of budget. Keep the best coefficients; at the end rebuild h at N=4000 from the best coefficients, optionally do a short final Nelder-Mead refinement at N=1000, and return the best.
experiments.prediction: If the optimal shape is smooth, this will reach R>0.70; if it stalls near 2/3, that is evidence the optimum is jagged or non-smooth.

plan.analysis: p0002 (0.8594) is the clear leader: N=50, symmetric, very flat f*f top (34.7% of knots within 1% of max), reached by a crude fixed-seed jitter search. F5 says flat f*f peak is the lever; F2 says low N wins; F6 leaves symmetry unresolved (p0007 found an asymmetric N=4000 shape). Bet 1: p0002's optimizer is weak, so a proper coordinate line-search at N=50 should push it further. Bet 2: the flat top may want a genuinely bimodal (two-block) f, not a unimodal bump. Bet 3: revisit the asymmetric p0007 branch at low N with p0002's search.

experiments.hypothesis: p0002's jitter hill climb is a weak optimizer; exact 1-D coordinate maximization on its symmetric N=50 shape will push R well past 0.859.
experiments.change: Take start (p0002's 50 heights), symmetrize h=(h+h[::-1])/2. Loop until 90% budget: for each index i=0..N-1 do an exact 1-D maximization of R over h_i only, using scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar with method='bounded' on [0, 4*max(h_i,0.1)] (R computed by the exact knot formula), update h_i to the argmax; do repeated sweeps. After each sweep, if no improvement >1e-6, apply a random multiplicative jitter (1+0.02*N(0,1)) to 3 random indices and keep going only if best improves; always retain the best-ever h. Return best h.
experiments.prediction: R >= 0.87, confirming p0002 was under-optimized and coordinate line-search is the right polish.

experiments.hypothesis: A flat f*f top may be produced by a genuinely bimodal f (two disjoint blocks with a gap) whose cross-term gives a trapezoidal flat plateau, beating a unimodal bump.
experiments.change: At N=50, build symmetric two-block profiles: h = 1 on steps [0,a) and [N-a,N), zero in the middle gap of width N-2a, for a grid a/N in {0.05,0.1,...,0.45}; also allow unequal block heights via a ratio grid {0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5,2.0}. Evaluate exact R for each. From the best two-block profile, run p0002's stochastic coordinate jitter search (multiplicative perturbations on 1..N/20 random indices, step_scale 0.05, 2% worse-acceptance, full 90% budget). Keep best over both the two-block grid and the search, and also evaluate start for reference; return the overall best.
experiments.prediction: If any two-block profile (before or after search) exceeds 0.86, the optimum f is non-unimodal; if all stay below 0.80, the unimodal bump is genuinely preferred.

experiments.hypothesis: p0007's asymmetric off-center shape is a real alternative optimum; resampled to low N and optimized with p0002's search it may beat the symmetric 0.859.
experiments.change: Resample p0007's construction to N=50 by bin-averaging (np.add.reduceat over 4000/50 groups), and also its mirror. Run p0002's stochastic coordinate jitter search (same perturbation/acceptance/step_scale schedule, 90% budget) seeded from each of these, plus one run seeded from start with small per-index asymmetric noise (multiply each entry by 1+0.05*N(0,1)) to allow symmetry breaking. Return the best R found among all runs and start.
experiments.prediction: If an asymmetric seed beats 0.87, the symmetric p0002 point is a local trap and F6 is answered 'asymmetric'; if all asymmetric seeds converge below 0.859, symmetry is confirmed.

plan.analysis: p0008 (0.8627) is the best; its gain came from a bimodal seed plus p0002's crude N=50 multiplicative jitter, and every 'smarter' optimizer (exact coordinate search, gradient ascent, L-BFGS at high N) does worse (F8, F10, F11-F13). So the winning lever is crude jitter at low resolution on a shape whose f*f top is flat (F5, F7). Two open questions: (a) is p0008 just one lucky jitter chain that more restarts/reheating could improve, and (b) is N=50 the sweet spot of the 'coarse grid regularizes' effect (F12)? I bet on refining the jitter search at N=50 plus probing resolution in both directions.

experiments.hypothesis: p0008 came from a single jitter chain; the jitter landscape around it has more room, so many short re-heated chains from perturbed copies of the best shape will find a better local optimum.
experiments.change: Keep p0008's _R and jitter code, but restructure the loop into ~30 segments: at the start of each segment set cur_h = best_h * (1 + 0.15*N(0,1) on all n entries, clipped at 0), cur_R = _R(cur_h), step_scale = 0.15; then run the existing jitter (k uniform in 1..n//20, multiplicative perturbation, 2% worse-acceptance) for a fixed slice of the remaining budget, with step_scale decaying *=0.999 each iteration down to 0.01. Keep the global best over all segments and return it. N stays 50, seed the first segment from start.
experiments.prediction: If p0008 was a single lucky chain, this multi-restart version exceeds 0.8630; if it stalls at ~0.8627, p0008 is already at the jitter-landscape optimum at N=50.

experiments.hypothesis: The N=50 grid may be binding: p0008's f*f plateau is flat to ~1% but the discrete heights limit further flattening, so the same crude jitter at N=100 seeded by an upsampled p0008 can push higher.
experiments.change: Upsample start (p0008's 50 heights) to N=100 by np.repeat(h, 2) (each step split into two equal steps; this preserves R exactly), then run p0008's jitter loop unchanged on n=100: k uniform in 1..max(2,n//20), multiplicative perturbation with step_scale starting at 0.05, 2% worse-acceptance, full 90% budget, return best-ever h (evaluate start itself first and keep it as fallback).
experiments.prediction: If the grid is the limit, N=100 reaches >=0.865; if it stays <=0.863, resolution is not the bottleneck and coarse N=50 is genuinely better.

experiments.hypothesis: F12's 'coarse grid regularizes' explanation predicts the opposite direction: an even coarser grid suppresses sharp spikes in f*f and gives a flatter top, so jitter at N=25 may beat N=50.
experiments.change: Downsample start to N=25 by averaging adjacent pairs (h25 = 0.5*(h[0::2]+h[1::2]), which preserves the step-function R when steps are paired), then run p0008's jitter loop at n=25 with step_scale starting at 0.08, k uniform in 1..max(2,n//10), 2% worse-acceptance, full 90% budget; also run the same loop from the current best N=50 shape's two other pairings-free variant: just the averaged seed, keep best-ever and return it.
experiments.prediction: If coarse regularization is real, N=25 exceeds 0.8627 despite fewer parameters; if it lands well below (<=0.85), N=50 is a genuine sweet spot and the jitter search, not the grid, is doing the work.
